heroText: Niamey is Niger's capital on the banks of the Niger River, a low-rise Sahelian city known for its riverside sunsets and lively markets. First-time visitors should browse the stalls of the Grand Marche, learn regional history and crafts at the National Museum of Niger, and watch pirogues cross the river at dusk. Diori Hamani International Airport connects the city to the region; check current travel advisories closely before planning any visit.

areas.name: Plateau
areas.text: Plateau is Niamey's central administrative district, home to government buildings, banks and many of the city's hotels.

areas.name: Grand Marche area
areas.text: The area around the Grand Marche is the city's commercial heart, packed with stalls, tailors and everyday shops.

areas.name: Riverside (Kalley)
areas.text: The riverside district along the Niger River offers restaurants and views popular for an evening walk or meal.

areas.name: Yantala
areas.text: Yantala is a quieter residential district favoured by diplomats and longer-stay visitors, north of the centre.

airports.text: Diori Hamani International Airport lies a few kilometres from the city centre; arrange transfers in advance given evolving security conditions.

stayOverview: Plateau offers the easiest first stay, close to hotels, banks and government offices, while the riverside area is best for an evening meal with Niger River views. Yantala provides a quieter, embassy-district alternative. Confirm current safety guidance before booking any Niamey trip.
hotelIntro: Plateau holds most of Niamey's established hotels within reach of the Grand Marche and National Museum, while Yantala suits diplomats and longer-stay visitors wanting a quieter residential setting.
rentalCars: Self-driving is not recommended given current security conditions; arrange a trusted local driver or pre-booked transfer instead.

history.label: Origins
history.text: Background and foundation The area of modern Niamey was of little importance before Niger's colonial era.
The first European mentions of Niamey were by the 1897 mission of Émile Auguste Léon Hourst, then the 1899 Voulet–Chanoine Mission, which set fire to Niamey.
Niamey had about 1,800 inhabitants in 1904, when it became the capital of the Third Military Territory of Niger.
The capital moved back to Zinder in 1911, after violence in the eastern region had subsided and reorganisation had drawn Niamey further away from the center of the territory.
As capital, Niamey also became the center for the educated class of mostly Songhai and Zarma people, with the first regional school opening in 1930.
Most residents wished to stay on the river bank, but, after a 1935 fire destroyed many straw buildings, they were forcibly moved to mudbrick houses, resulting in multiethnic neighbourhoods.
Despite this, housing insecurity increased, and the informal settlement of Talladjé was created in 1966.
On 9 April 1999, Baré was ambushed, shot, and killed at Niamey's airport during a coup d'état.
In 2013, American and French military bases were established at adjacent parts of Diori Hamani International Airport.
